titulo.texto: The Reflecting Pool and Bronze Conch

frase_gancho.texto: A piece of the ancient lake, right in the courtyard.

puente_narrativo.texto: With the water behind you, it is time to begin the tour in order. Head to Hall 1: before the gods and the cities comes a bigger question, who are we and where do we come from?

guion_corto.texto: In front of the entrance to the Mexica Hall, the courtyard becomes a pond. It is a mirror of water with aquatic plants, a small evocation of Lake Texcoco, the water on which Tenochtitlan was built, the city you are about to meet. At the center stands a bronze sculpture shaped like a sea snail shell, titled “Sol del Viento,” the work of Íker Larrauri. For the ancient Mexicans, the cut conch shell was an emblem of Ehécatl, the god of the wind, and conch trumpets sounded in ceremonies and in war. Lean over the water: it reflects the sky, The Umbrella and the walls of the museum. Use it as a pause before moving on.

guion_largo.texto:
It is hard to imagine today, but Mexico City was born in the middle of a lake. When the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, on a small island, the valley was full of water: connected lakes, canals, floating chinampas where maize and flowers were grown. The Spanish drained the system over the centuries, and today the water lies beneath the asphalt. Only a few pieces survive, such as the canals of Xochimilco, south of the city, where crops are still grown on chinampas. This pond is a memory of all that.

And it is no coincidence that it stands right here. The museum rises in Chapultepec, and on Chapultepec hill sprang the springs that carried fresh water to Tenochtitlan by an aqueduct, because the water of the lake was brackish. Anyone who drank water in the Mexica capital, to a great extent, drank from this forest.

Pause on the scale of time, because this lake did not begin with the Mexica. Later, in the Peopling of the Americas Hall, you will see how a mammoth was trapped in the mud of one of its shores some eleven thousand years ago. In the Preclassic Hall, a model will show the village of Cuicuilco, on the edge of the same valley. And in the Mexica Hall you will see how the life of an entire city depended on water. The lake was the stage for all the history you are about to walk through.

Now look at the bronze shell, the work of Íker Larrauri, the artist and museum designer who made many of the museum’s murals and dioramas. The sea snail shell had an enormous presence in Mesoamerica. It was blown like a trumpet to call warriors, to announce rituals and to greet the dawn. A shell cut in cross-section, with its spiral in view, was also the emblem of Ehécatl-Quetzalcóatl, the wind god who swept the roads so that the rains could arrive. That is why here, beside the water, the shell is a kind of warning: the wind comes before the rain. Later you will meet Tecciztécatl, the god of the moon, whose name means “the one of the conch.”

Spend a few seconds before the still surface. The museum is reflected in it, down there the shadows of The Umbrella float, and in the distance you can make out the entrance to the Mexica Hall. Ramírez Vázquez wanted that reflection to be not an ornament but an invitation to look at the building as one looked at a city on the water: with the feeling that, beneath what you see, there is another layer of history.

And one more invitation: when you enter the Mexica Hall, try to remember this pond. You will see that the Templo Mayor rose on an island surrounded by water, that its causeways floated over the lake, and that the gods of rain and wind, Tláloc and Ehécatl, had a temple of their own. What you are about to see inside began out here. Even war, for the Mexica, was spoken with a word of water: “atl-tlachinolli,” water and fire together. In the Mexica Hall you will see it carved in stone.

texto: Find the bronze shell at the center of the pond and follow its spiral with your eyes
Observe the water plants growing in the pond
Lean over the water and find the reflection of The Umbrella

texto.Culture: Modern Mexican plastic integration: Pedro Ramírez Vázquez (pond design) and Íker Larrauri (sculpture “Sol del Viento”)
texto.Material: Stone-lined pond with lake flora (cattails, papyrus and water lilies), a gas burner set in a stepped fret motif, and a bronze sculpture
texto.Location: Eastern end of the Central Courtyard, in front of the Mexica Hall

texto.pregunta: Myth: The pond in the courtyard is just a decorative pool.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It evokes Lake Texcoco, the watery landscape on which Tenochtitlan was founded.
